items.abstract: OFFICIAL DESCRIPTION OF THE SCIENTIFIC WORK | INTERNATIONAL CATALOG 2026 RESEARCH TITLE: BUILD OR DESTROY: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE TRANSFORMATIVE POTENTIAL AND DISINFORMATION RISKS OF MODERN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE LEAD RESEARCHER: Dr. Dieudelin Arcangel Legrand - Brotherswagg Robert Academic Jurisdiction and Country of Origin: Republic of Haiti PRIMARY PUBLISHING HOUSE: BrotherswaggStudioRecords Publishing (BSR Publishing) / TM3 MUSIC GROUP INSTITUTIONAL CORPORATE AUTHORSHIP, APPROVAL AND EDITORIAL REVIEW ENDORSEMENT: International Institutional Academic Editorial Committee (IIAEC) and its International Research Consortium: - The Hellenic Institute (Critical Thinking and Theoretical Frameworks) - The Atlantic Research Group (Factual Analysis and Global Perspective) - The Euro-Academic Council (Literary Standards and European Editorial Review) - The Oxbridge Academic (Methodological Rigor and Technical Review) - The Continental Bureau (Source Documentation and Multilingual Research) INTERNATIONAL EDITION: November 2026 ORIGINAL LANGUAGE OF PUBLICATION: Spanish (Official Master Edition) --- 1. SCIENTIFIC CLASSIFICATION AND EPISTEMOLOGICAL NATURE OF THE WORK This publication belongs to the genre of the Critical Review Scientific Article, Epistemological Analysis, and Technological Foresight (an In-Depth Argumentative Scientific Essay). By virtue of its interdisciplinary structure, the work is classified within the fields of Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, and Philosophy of Technology, while establishing direct analytical connections with Communication Studies, Digital Sociology, Applied Ethics, Cognitive Psychology of Perception, and Cyber Law. Having undergone a rigorous process of methodological auditing and structural verification under the standards of the International Institutional Academic Editorial Committee (IIAEC), this research distinguishes itself from conventional technical literature through its comprehensive scope and unwavering commitment to empirical truth. It is neither a merely descriptive manual nor a speculative pamphlet, but rather a reference work designed to diagnose, with surgical precision, the most consequential technological phenomenon of our time. 2. WHY THIS WORK IS ESSENTIAL READING IN THE 21ST CENTURY Humanity is experiencing a historic moment in which the boundary between the real and the artificial has been erased by the speed of algorithms. Every day, millions of people interact with texts, voices, photographs, and video sequences that appear to reflect authentic events but have actually been entirely fabricated by generative artificial intelligence systems. Faced with this unprecedented reality, global society oscillates between two equally dangerous extremes: naïve fascination with the power of machines and uninformed panic in the face of a technology that few people fully understand. "Build or Destroy: A Critical Analysis of the Transformative Potential and Disinformation Risks of Modern Artificial Intelligence" was conceived to dispel this conceptual fog. This work confronts readers with an unavoidable question: How is it possible that the same technology capable of saving lives in medicine, accelerating scientific discoveries, and democratizing education has simultaneously become the preferred tool of countless digital content creators for falsifying reality, impersonating identities, and monetizing deception on a planetary scale? Through rigorous, direct, transparent prose, free from corporate constraints, the Lead Researcher, Dr. Dieudelin Arcangel Legrand - Brotherswagg Robert, together with the IIAEC collegiate body and BSR Publishing, exposes the hidden mechanisms behind this duality without barriers or concealment. Readers who explore these pages will encounter documented truths about how the attention economy operates, why digital platforms amplify synthetic falsehoods, and how society can defend its right to truth without renouncing scientific progress. 3. THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE WORK: AN EVOLUTIONARY NARRATIVE IN FOUR FOUNDATIONAL MODULES To provide a progressive, logical, and deeply enriching reading experience, this research has been structured into seven sections organized around four foundational modules that evolve as one continuous scientific narrative: - FIRST FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | Recent Evolution and Future Horizons of AI: Guides readers from the origins of symbolic computing to the transformer revolution, multimodal foundation models, and emerging autonomous agentic systems, clearly explaining how machines acquired the ability to synthesize realities indistinguishable from the physical world. - SECOND FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | The Constructive and Transformative Potential: Rigorously documents the positive side of this revolution, demonstrating how artificial intelligence is transforming medical diagnosis, drug design, climate sustainability, space research, the inclusion of persons with disabilities, and the democratization of knowledge in every corner of the planet. - THIRD FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | The Anatomy of Deception and a Critical Examination of Malicious Use: Constitutes the critical and revealing core of the manuscript. It examines with intellectual courage how numerous unscrupulous content creators exploit AI to manufacture deepfakes, clone human voices, fabricate pseudo-scientific or pseudo-journalistic evidence, and operate artificial engagement farms, thereby undermining the historical principle of audiovisual evidence and profiting from public credulity. - FOURTH FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | Ethical Discussion, Governance, and the Future of Trust: Proposes concrete solutions to the epistemic crisis by establishing the principles of mandatory transparency, cryptographic traceability from the point of origin, the legal shared responsibility of digital platforms, and the urgent need for critical literacy among citizens. 4. RELEVANCE TO UNIVERSITIES, RESEARCHERS, STUDENTS, AND SOCIETY This work has been conceived as an indispensable reference resource for multiple sectors of the global community: - For Researchers and Academics: It offers an interdisciplinary theoretical framework integrating algorithmic engineering, epistemology, and digital sociology, supported by cutting-edge technical references and international standards. - For Universities and Academic Institutions: It constitutes a bibliographic resource of significant educational value for courses in technological ethics, social communication, computer science, digital law, and contemporary philosophy. - For Students and Young Creators: It provides a moral and technical compass for understanding the power of the tools at their disposal, inspiring them to use artificial intelligence to build genuine knowledge and reject the culture of digital fraud. - For Citizens, Journalists, and the General Public: It delivers the practical and conceptual tools necessary to protect independent judgment against media manipulation and distinguish genuine progress from synthetic illusion. 5. A UNIVERSAL INVITATION: A WORK FOR EVERYONE, BREAKING DOWN BARRIERS AND BUILDING KNOWLEDGE WITHOUT BORDERS Beyond its methodological rigor and technical soundness, this research carries a fundamental declaration of principles: genuine scientific knowledge does not belong to closed elites or intellectual monopolies; it belongs to all humanity. For far too long, the production and validation of global knowledge have been concentrated within hermetic academic canons that erected invisible barriers—geographical, economic, linguistic, and racial—to determine who had the right to conduct research, publish, and be heard. Conceived in the Republic of Haiti with a global outlook and supported by the alliance between BrotherswaggStudioRecords Publishing (BSR Publishing) / TM3 MUSIC GROUP and the International Institutional Academic Editorial Committee (IIAEC), this work deliberately breaks through these historical barriers. It demonstrates that cutting-edge critical thinking, scientific excellence, and the ethical defense of truth can and must emerge from the Global South and reach the entire world, engaging in dialogue on equal terms with institutions across every nation. For this reason, an open, fraternal, and universal invitation is extended to all readers, students, professors, universities, independent researchers, artists, journalists, and citizens of every nation, origin, and circumstance: this work belongs to you. Every page of this study contains essential truths for understanding the world in which we live and defending the future we share. The entire global community is invited to read this article with a critical mindset, debate its arguments in classrooms and across digital networks, cite its findings, translate its message, and actively contribute to the development of an open, inclusive body of scientific literature, free from intellectual racism and committed to human dignity. Because only when knowledge is freed from chains and shared without exclusion does science fulfill its noblest purpose: to illuminate the minds of all human beings. items.title: Cognitive Cross-Pollination among AI Developers, Industry Application Integrators, and Beneficiaries in a Future AGI & ASI Society
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aims to conceptualise a Three-Level Cognitive Cross-Pollination Model involving AI Developers and Controllers, Industry Application Integrators, and AI Beneficiaries in a hypothetical future Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) society. It seeks to explore multidirectional knowledge exchange, stakeholder collaboration, and governance mechanisms to promote responsible AI innovation, equitable benefit distribution, and sustainable human-centred societal development. Methodology: This study adopts an exploratory, qualitative, literature-based conceptual research approach, drawing upon secondary sources to examine cognitive cross-pollination among three stakeholder groups in a hypothetical future AGI and ASI society. It employs SWOC, ABCD, PESTLE, qualitative predictive scenario analysis, and impact analysis to evaluate the proposed model's technological, organisational, ethical, economic, and societal implications. Analysis/Result: The integrated SWOC, ABCD, PESTLE, predictive scenario, and impact analyses highlight the potential strengths, opportunities, benefits, constraints, and challenges of cognitive cross-pollination among the three stakeholder groups in a future AGI and ASI society. The findings suggest that multidirectional knowledge exchange, stakeholder collaboration, continuous feedback, and responsible governance could promote technological innovation, industrial integration, equitable benefit distribution, and sustainable human-centred societal development. Originality/Value: This study proposes a novel Three-Level Cognitive Cross-Pollination Model that integrates AI Developers and Controllers, Industry Application Integrators, and AI Beneficiaries into a unified conceptual framework for a hypothetical future AGI and ASI society. Its originality lies in examining multidirectional knowledge exchange and stakeholder interdependence through integrated SWOC, ABCD, PESTLE, predictive scenario, and impact analyses, offering valuable insights into responsible AI governance, collaborative innovation, and sustainable human-centred development. Type of Paper: Exploratory Research Analysis

items.title: Designing Cognitive Scaffolds for Generative-AI-Assisted Introductory Programming
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make introductory programming tasks easier to complete, but a working program is not evidence of durable learning. This conceptual-theoretical paper integrates research on cognitive load, metacognition, self-explanation, productive failure, appropriate reliance on automation, and recent studies of AI-assisted programming to propose a five-phase cognitive-scaffolding framework. Learners first make an unaided attempt, request bounded assistance, verify the response against requirements and independently designed tests, explain the mechanism and calibrate confidence, and then complete a related transfer task as support fades. AI literacy, ethical disclosure, privacy, and instructor orchestration operate across all phases. The framework identifies process evidence that remains inspectable when generated code is available, including problem representations, hypotheses, verification records, explanations, confidence judgments, and unaided transfer. It also states six testable propositions and an evaluation blueprint for introductory programming courses. The contribution is a bounded design logic, not a claim that the sequence has already been validated: GenAI should reduce avoidable burden while leaving consequential decisions, checks, and explanations with the learner.

items.title: Designing metacognitive scaffolding in flipped learning to enhance students’ visual–spatial reasoning: Evidence from geometry instruction
items.abstract: The development of students’ visual–spatial reasoning is a persistent challenge in geometry learning, where abstract representations and spatial transformations require high levels of cognitive engagement. Although flipped learning has been widely implemented to promote active learning, its effectiveness largely depends on the quality of instructional design and pedagogical support provided during in-class activities. This study investigates how metacognitive scaffolding can be intentionally designed and embedded within flipped learning to enhance students’ visual–spatial reasoning. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed in secondary geometry instruction involving 62 students assigned to experimental and control groups. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-tests of visual–spatial reasoning, while qualitative data were obtained from classroom observations and semi-structured teacher interviews. The results indicate that students who experienced metacognitive scaffolding within a flipped learning environment demonstrated significantly greater gains in visual–spatial reasoning than those in a conventional flipped classroom, with a large effect size. Qualitative findings further reveal that scaffolding prompts supported students’ planning, monitoring, and reflective evaluation during problem-solving activities. Overall, the findings suggest that flipped learning environments become more cognitively productive when structured metacognitive scaffolding is deliberately incorporated into the learning design.

items.title: Digital enablement and employee performance in society 5.0: a dual-path model of motivation and exhaustion
items.abstract: Introduction Society 5.0 integrates advanced digital technologies with human-centered work systems, yet its implications for sustainable employee performance remain underexplored. Drawing on Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examines the relationship between Society 5.0 enablement intensity (S5EI) and sustainable human performance through autonomous motivation and emotional exhaustion, considering human-centric governance capability as a moderator. Methods The study employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyse data collected from 519 employees working in digitally intensive sectors in India. Results The findings indicate that S5EI is positively associated with sustainable human performance, primarily through autonomous motivation. Emotional exhaustion partially offsets this positive effect through competitive mediation. Human-centric governance capability strengthens the relationship between autonomous motivation and sustainable human performance but does not significantly buffer the negative effect of emotional exhaustion. Discussion The findings conceptualize digital enablement as a dual-valence work condition that simultaneously strengthens autonomy-based motivation and increases digital demands, integrating Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of participatory digital governance, workload management, and employee recovery measures for supporting sustainable human performance.

items.title: Digital Transformation Through a Socio‐Technical Systems Lens: Women Leaders' Approaches to Technological Change and Organizational Dynamics
items.abstract: Organizations navigating digital transformation face persistent challenges integrating social and technical elements to support innovation and worker wellbeing. Despite increasing workforce participation, women remain underrepresented in senior leadership roles that shape how this integration occurs, leaving perspectives shaped by gendered organizational experience underexplored within digital transformation research. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with sixteen senior women leaders across Australian organizations, this study applies socio‐technical systems theory and a gender‐informed leadership perspective to examine how these leaders understood and navigated the relationship between technical and social domains during digital transformation. Participants treated technical and social considerations as mutually constitutive, enacting their integration through communication, employee participation, human‐centered work design, capability development and ongoing adaptation. Psychosocial safety emerged across technical, social and integration‐focused accounts as a system‐level condition implicated in this process. Together, these findings provide an empirical account of human‐centric transformation within Industry 5.0 and extend socio‐technical systems theory by conceptualizing integration as an enacted process through which technical and social considerations continually shape one another. A gender‐informed analysis further demonstrates the value of gendered organizational experience for understanding how socio‐technical integration is accomplished in practice.

items.title: Does Generative AI Reduce Mental Effort at The Expense of Deep Thinking? An Experimental Investigation of Cognitive Load and Knowledge Retention
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.

items.title: Effect of Facilitated Problem-Based Learning on Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation Among Nursing Students in North-East Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated the effect of facilitated Problem-Based Learning (PBL) on intrinsic and extrinsic motivation among nursing students in North-East Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test control group design was adopted. The population comprised 1,065 ND II nursing students from six Colleges of Nursing Science in North-East Nigeria, from which 200 students were selected using a multi-stage sampling procedure. The sample consisted of 100 students in the experimental group exposed to facilitated PBL and 100 students in the control group taught using conventional lecture-based instruction. Data were collected using a 28-item Academic Motivation Questionnaire (AMQ). The instrument demonstrated satisfactory reliability with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.84. The experimental group participated in a six-week facilitated PBL intervention involving nursing-related case scenarios, guided questioning, collaborative learning, feedback, and self-directed learning activities. Data were analyzed using means, standard deviations, and t-tests at the 0.05 level of significance. Finding showed that the experimental group recorded an increase in mean intrinsic-motivation scores from 26.30 at pre-test to 50.30 at post-test, compared with an increase from 25.90 to 30.20 in the control group. A significant effect was also found on extrinsic motivation, with the experimental group recording a greater reduction in extrinsic motivation than the control group, t(198) = 8.72, p < .05. therefore, motivation also differed significantly between the facilitated PBL and lecture groups, t(198) = 14.02, p < .001. Furthermore, a significant difference was observed between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, t(198) = 6.85, p < .001. The study concluded that facilitated PBL is an effective instructional approach for strengthening intrinsic motivation and promoting more self-directed learning among nursing students. It was recommended that nursing institutions should integrate facilitated PBL into their programmes, train educators in effective PBL facilitation, provide adequate learning resources, and emphasize learning activities that foster students’ intrinsic motivation.

items.title: El Rol Humano en la Automatización Inteligente de Procesos Administrativos con IA generativa: Revisión Crítica de la Literatura
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents are entering administrative processes. This marks a shift from robotic process automation to intelligent automation and raises the question of what role people keep when systems process, analyze, and make decisions. The objective was to critically analyze the literature from 2020 to 2026 on the competencies that are transformed or emerging, and on research trends and gaps. A critical and integrative documentary study was carried out in Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, Redalyc, Dialnet, and Google Scholar. It included peer-reviewed studies in Spanish and English, which were analyzed with an extraction matrix and a thematic synthesis. Based on the reviewed literature, GenAI cuts writing time by up to 40% and raises productivity by 15%, especially among novices. However, greater trust in it reduces critical thinking. The emerging competencies are data analysis, digital and complex cognitive skills, decision-making, and continuous learning. Qualitative and short-term studies predominate. There are gaps in the quality of oversight, in Latin American contexts, SMEs, and the public sector, and in the development of expertise. The human role is shifting from execution to oversight and governance. It is effective only under adequate conditions and complying with a protocol is not enough.

items.title: Emotionally Aware AI Chatbots for Adolescents: A Review of Psychological Principles for Learning, Calibrated Trust, and Healthy Human–AI Interaction
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

items.title: Employee Adaptability In The Digital Workplace: A Systematic Literature Review Of Individual And Organizational Determinants
items.abstract: Digital transformation, remote and hybrid work, and the diffusion of artificial intelligence have made employee adaptability a critical organizational capability, yet research on its antecedents remains fragmented across psychology, information systems, and management. This study aims to synthesize evidence on the individual and organizational determinants of employee adaptability in the digital workplace. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and ABI/INFORM for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025, and findings were integrated through thematic synthesis. The review shows that adaptability is conceptualized as a multidimensional capability spanning cognitive, behavioral, and emotional responses to technological change. Individual determinants include dispositional traits, self-efficacy and digital competence, career adaptability, and attitudes toward change, whereas organizational determinants include leadership and change communication, psychological safety, training, job and technology design, and flexible work arrangements. The literature suggests that these determinants operate as interacting resources, with supportive organizational conditions amplifying individual capacity. An integrative framework and a research agenda emphasizing longitudinal, multilevel, and emerging-economy studies are proposed. The findings guide managers and human resource practitioners in designing workplaces that support adaptation.

items.title: Ergonomic issues in vertical farming systems: a PRISMA-informed narrative review
items.abstract: Vertical farming (VF) represents a transformative approach to agricultural production utilizing multi-tiered, controlled-environment systems, yet it introduces unique ergonomic challenges distinct from conventional agriculture. This literature review synthesizes current evidence on ergonomic issues in vertical farming systems, alongside evidence from indoor farming and broader controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) systems, examining musculoskeletal disorder (MSD) prevalence, risk factors, assessment methodologies, and intervention strategies. Agricultural workers in greenhouse and indoor farming environments experience MSD prevalence rates of 50.9% to 89.3%, with the lower back, shoulders, knees, and neck most commonly affected. Available evidence suggests that vertical farming may present distinctive ergonomic challenges, including multi-tiered configurations associated with overhead reaching, lower-tier access constraints, repetitive precision tasks, environmental stressors, and complex human-technology interactions. However, much of the current evidence is inferred from greenhouse and broader controlled-environment agriculture systems. While traditional ergonomic assessment tools (RULA, REBA, OWAS) and advanced methods (EMG) have been applied in agricultural contexts, their adaptation to vertical farming remains limited. Current interventions show promise through workspace optimization, tool redesign, automation, and participatory ergonomics approaches. However, significant knowledge gaps persist regarding longitudinal health outcomes, human-automation interaction, cognitive ergonomics, and socioeconomic dimensions specific to vertical farming. This review highlights the emerging need for human-centered design principles in VF system development to ensure worker health, safety, and operational sustainability.

items.title: Ergonomics-Integrated Generative AI for Personalized Work Design in Aging and Diversifying Industrial Workforces
items.abstract: In industrialized countries, rapid population aging and declining birth rates have made labor shortages a critical issue in industrial workplaces. Without actively utilizing elderly workers, persons with disabilities, and foreign workers, on-site operations risk becoming unsustainable. Addressing this challenge requires not only technological innovation but also a transdisciplinary engineering approach that integrates human, social, and industrial system perspectives. This study proposes a personalized work design framework that combines generative artificial intelligence (AI) and ergonomics to enable inclusive and sustainable industrial operations. The proposed framework utilizes individual attribute data—such as age-related physical characteristics, functional limitations, work experience, and language proficiency—to generate task configurations tailored to diverse worker groups. Ergonomic principles are systematically embedded into the generative AI model to adapt task sequences, work postures, workload distribution, and operational instructions according to individual capabilities and constraints. From an engineering perspective, the framework integrates data-driven AI modeling, human factors engineering, and production system design to dynamically optimize the interaction between workers and industrial environments. A case study conducted in a manufacturing-related setting demonstrates that the proposed approach reduces physical strain and cognitive workload while maintaining or improving productivity and operational stability. The results indicate that AI-driven ergonomic task personalization is particularly effective in enabling the participation of elderly workers, persons with disabilities, and foreign workers in on-site industrial work. This research highlights the value of transdisciplinary engineering in addressing complex societal challenges posed by demographic change. By bridging generative AI, ergonomics, and industrial engineering, the proposed framework provides a scalable and human-centered solution for designing adaptive workplaces and supporting long-term workforce sustainability in aging and diversifying societies.

items.title: Exploring the Interplay Between Stress, Reflexivity, and Professional Development in Pre-Service Teachers
items.abstract: This article reports on an empirical study conducted among a cohort of pre-service teachers, aimed at enhancing their professional competencies within a university teacher training institute. Grounded in the theoretical and methodological framework of professional didactics, this research investigates how analyzing professional situations contributes to skill acquisition and psychological well-being. The variables measured throughout this inquiry include classroom management skills, individual reflective capacity, and situational stress perceived by the participants. The quantitative and qualitative findings reveal a statistically weak correlation between reflexivity and the development of professional competencies. Crucially, the data demonstrate no significant relationship between a teacher's reflective capacity and their level of perceived situational stress. These results suggest that while fostering reflexivity helps to enhance professional competencies and pedagogical reasoning, it is inherently insufficient to reduce the psychological burden and stress experienced by novice teachers in the classroom. Consequently, this study argues that professional training frameworks cannot rely solely on reflexive analysis to ensure occupational health. To bridge this gap, teacher education programs would significantly benefit from integrating explicit stress management practices, emotional regulation techniques, and coping strategies directly into their core curricula. By doing so, training institutes could offer a more holistic approach, combining cognitive professional development with the psychological resilience necessary for sustainable teaching careers.

items.title: External resilience controls as sociotechnical governance: an extension of dynamic capabilities theory under externally driven volatility
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how organizations construct governance responses to externally driven volatility by embedding external signals into control practices. Focusing on climate exposed agricultural firms, this study extends dynamic capabilities theory (DCT) by developing external resilience controls (ERCs) as a sociotechnical governance construct that illuminates how firms make volatility actionable through formal control routines. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a pragmatic constructivist design science orientation, this study combines six years of financial and operational context (2019–2024) with a longitudinal interpretive content analysis of annual report and sustainability disclosures (2022–2024) from five major agricultural firms. An interpretive design approach enables the systematic synthesis of disclosed organizational practices into a conceptual framework. Findings ERCs emerge as sociotechnical governance arrangements that translate external volatility into organizationally meaningful routines and actionable dynamic capabilities. These arrangements materialize through digital sensing infrastructures, traceability systems, scenario thresholds and board-level oversight that collectively shape how firms interpret and respond to climate anomalies, regulatory shifts and technological change. ERCs reveal resilience as an ongoing process of constructing, stabilizing and legitimizing responses to external volatility. Practical implications ERCs offer practitioners an analytic framework to operationalize dynamic capabilities by integrating digital tools and governance structures. They show how firms convert external volatility into actionable sensing, seizing and reconfiguring routines, enabling adaptive decision-making without relying on rigid control mechanisms. Originality/value This study advances qualitative management scholarship by conceptualizing ERCs as sociotechnical governance constructs. It contributes to strategy research by extending DCT, showing how dynamic capabilities are enacted through the interplay of digital infrastructures, institutional pressures, and organizational sensemaking.

items.title: Farol do conhecimento: localização de expertise e conexão profissionalna gestão do conhecimento da Petrobras
items.abstract: This article analyzes the Knowledge Lighthouse, the name Petrobras gives to the knowledge management practice commonly known as Yellow Pages. The solution is a business intelligence dashboard that integrates corporate data and professional records to locate expertise by knowledge area or by person. A qualitative and descriptive approach was adopted through a single case study and bibliographic and documentary analysis. The theoretical framework combines knowledge management, transactive memory, competence mapping, intellectual capital, communities of practice, and sociotechnical systems. The study describes the dashboard’s conception, its SAP/SIRH data sources, daily D-1 updating, search and profile detail views, query paths, and corporate access. The analytical findings indicate that the solution may improve expert findability, reduce search costs, foster learning and knowledge integration, and support critical knowledge management, team formation, innovation, internal mobility, succession, and organizational memory. items.title: From BIM to Digital Twin-Enabled Facility Management: A Decision-Support Framework for Complex Healthcare Buildings
items.abstract: Healthcare Facility Management depends on information distributed across Building Information Models (BIMs), operational sensor systems, and multiple organizational actors, yet the transition from BIM-organized asset representation to a decision-supporting, Digital-Twin-enabled environment remains insufficiently operationalized. This study develops and instantiates a management-oriented framework for this transition through a literature-informed, case-derived design at a complex hospital surgical department. Evidence was classified by maturity level and cross-mapped across six information-and-decision layers: Asset Information, Operational Data, Integration and Information Management, Facility Management Process, Decision Support, and Organizational and Governance. The framework was instantiated against two documented prototype-level sensor subsystems. The scientific contribution is a traceable mapping from case evidence and literature requirements to six information-and-decision layers, making the boundary between demonstrated outputs and unobserved human action explicit. The managerial contribution is a cross-layer requirement matrix and a five-phase roadmap with auditable progression gates, linking each information requirement to a responsible role and a maintenance decision. The evidence comprises a documented information environment, functioning sensor prototypes, and integration tested in a virtual environment with real sensor data. The framework offers healthcare Facility Management practitioners a planning instrument for preparing and assessing the transition; practitioner assessment, multi-case testing, and longitudinal hospital deployment are its next validation stages.

items.title: From extension to the reconfiguration of the human: artificial intelligence as an environment in media ecology
items.abstract: Purpose The main objective is to analyze the sociotechnical implications of Artificial Intelligence as it transitions from an assistive model (“copilot”) to an agentic and autonomous model. It seeks to explore how this new environment redefines human identity, authorship, and the autonomy of thought in the face of total technical integration. Method The study employs a theoretical-critical analysis methodology based on Media Ecology as a metadiscipline. It adopts a systemic and longitudinal perspective that traces the evolution of human interfaces from the control of fire to the present. As a primary diagnostic tool, it uses the McLuhan Tetrad to examine what AI enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into. Findings AI as an Exocortex: AI functions as an external layer of brain processing that tends to reshape our decisions, tastes, and analyses. Autonomous and Agentic Model: Unlike previous media that functioned as a human reflection, AI contributes to creating an autonomous model capable of generating culture and narratives independently. The “Black Box” Effect: The inscrutable nature of neural networks hinders transparency and oversight in critical areas like justice or healthcare. Displacement of Judgment: There is a progressive “anesthesia” where human critical judgment is displaced toward automated algorithmic processes. Implications Cognitive Amputation: By delegating decision-making and technical labor to machines, humans risk the atrophy of their own critical and creative capacities. Crisis of Truth: AI can “hack” the operating system of civilization (language), creating “reality bubbles” where “truth” becomes a byproduct of the algorithm rather than human dialectics. Dictatorship of Efficiency: The velocity of AI exceeds the response capacity of democratic institutions, potentially rendering “freedom of choice” an obsolete concept in favor of automated efficiency. Value The text provides a critical outlook that moves beyond technical optimism, proposing an “ethics of selective disconnection”. Its value lies in defending human imperfection, ambiguity, and silence as essential non-optimizable elements that must be preserved against the binary logic of AI.

items.title: From Ujrāh to Algorithmic Accountability: Reconstructing Wage Justice and Human Dignity in the Platform Economy
items.abstract: Digital labour platforms increasingly organise work through algorithmic systems that allocate tasks, monitor performance, determine access to income-generating opportunities, calculate remuneration, and impose sanctions. These systems may reduce coordination costs and expand market access, yet they also create distinctive problems of wage justice when workers cannot understand the rules governing earnings, verify deductions, contest adverse decisions, or identify the institution responsible for algorithmic outcomes. This article develops a critical-conceptual framework that reconstructs the Islamic concept of ujrāh for the governance of remuneration in the platform economy. It integrates scholarship on algorithmic management and platform labour, organisational justice, labour regulation, and Islamic jurisprudence on ijārah and ethical remuneration. The analysis proceeds through conceptual mapping, normative interpretation, institutional translation, and framework synthesis. It argues that ujrāh should not be confined to the nominal amount agreed for a task; its contemporary ethical assessment must also encompass the procedures and infrastructures through which work is allocated, remuneration is calculated, and payment rights are enforced. The article proposes five interdependent dimensions of Islamic algorithmic wage justice: distributive fairness; contractual intelligibility; algorithmic explainability and contestability; equitable allocation of economic risk; and protection of human dignity and worker agency. The framework contributes to platform-work scholarship by connecting distributive and procedural justice with a normative account of contractual responsibility grounded in Islamic economic ethics. It is conceptual and requires empirical testing across platform sectors and regulatory settings.

items.title: From Vision to Interaction: Evaluating Dynamic Social Intelligence of VLM Agents in ALIVE-World
items.abstract: As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.

items.title: Gamified Resistance and the Reproduction of Platform Control: Jiacan in China's Food‐Delivery Sector
items.abstract: This article examines Jiacan , Chinese food‐delivery riders' term for retaining or consuming undelivered food. Drawing on digital ethnography of rider chat groups, interviews, Douyin vlogs and public discussion threads, it shows how grievance‐linked Jiacan acquires resistant meaning through customer‐mediated disputes, digital circulation and peer evaluation. We develop Gamified Resistance to describe resistance socially organised through shared procedures, risk–reward calculations and judgments about acceptable conduct. The analysis identifies three pathways through which resistance may reproduce platform control: proceduralised rule‐navigation, triadic displacement toward customers and priced dissent. Riders can obtain immediate relief or retaliation while sustaining dependence on platform adjudication, customer‐mediated relations and sanctions. Control reproduction remains provisional: peer judgments, public scrutiny and customer claims can regulate participation and channel disputes, but also challenge the practice or redirect conflict toward the platform.

items.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
items.abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

items.title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
items.abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

items.title: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
items.abstract: Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

items.title: How to Translate Ergonomics Findings into Design-Relevant Principles in an Ergodesign Framework: The Case of Lohr Industrie
items.abstract: Aligning human capabilities with system requirements is crucial for lowering injury risks and enhancing performance in industrial settings like the assembly of automobiles. In this context, we define the Ergodesign Framework as a structure for integrating ergonomics and its findings, Ergodesign and its generation of principles, and design and its pursuit of technical solutions within a transdisciplinary, continuous, and bidirectional process. In this paper, we focus on the internal Ergodesign process, whose objective is to translate ergonomic data into design-relevant principles that can subsequently be applied during design phases, thereby enabling the proactive implementation of ergonomic requirements. The process is based on the capitalization of recurring issues observed during ergonomic analyses, the identification of their root causes, and the definition of Ergodesign rules, making it possible to create a database of Ergodesign principles that can be applied by designers. This process is implemented within the company Lohr Industrie, where standardized elements were developed to define internal rules for product and process design, based on findings from ergonomic studies conducted across different workshops. items.title: Human and Ethical Factors in AI- and IoT-Driven Industry 5.0 Smart Manufacturing: A PRISMA-Guided Systematic and Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) are promoted as the technological backbone of Industry 5.0, which re-centres manufacturing on human well-being, resilience, and sustainability. This PRISMA 2020-guided review combines bibliometric analysis with narrative synthesis to examine how the human and ethical dimensions of AI- and IoT-driven smart manufacturing are addressed. Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore searches without a start-year limit identified 1904 unique records; all were coded at abstract level (647 eligible records), and 86 prioritized records were synthesized in full text around five research questions: ethical risk, human factors, operationalization of human-centricity, governance, and the technology-readiness gap. Performance, thematic-evolution, co-citation, usage, and readership analyses complement the synthesis. Human-factors and architecture research dominate, yet reviews and conceptual papers prevail, and only 10% of eligible records report industrial validation. Ethical risk is the fastest-growing theme but is operationalized mainly as explainability. Governance is the primary object of 2.8% of eligible records, and its intellectual base is thin: about 3% of these studies cite the EU AI Act, the GDPR, or AI-law scholarship. A human-centric Industry 5.0 maturity model and a research agenda are proposed.

items.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
items.abstract: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

items.title: Human-AI Collaborative Decision Framework for Distributed Aircraft Power Management in Flight Test Operations
items.abstract: During flight test operations, distributed aircraft power systems are typically managed by human operators through centralized monitoring interfaces. Operators must balance system health, mission objectives, and safety margins under dynamically changing test conditions. However, existing systems are largely reactive and primarily provide fault alerts without predictive insight, which can delay timely intervention and increase operator cognitive workload. This paper proposes a human-AI collaborative decision framework for distributed aircraft power management in flight test environments. The framework integrates predictive health assessment, risk modeling, and strategy evaluation to support operator decision making. A lightweight prognostic mechanism continuously estimates the health risk of individual power cabinets using electrical and thermal indicators. Based on the predicted risk, the system identifies high-risk modules and recommends a small set of feasible power management strategies that balance risk mitigation and mission impact. Human operators remain responsible for final decision selection through a human-centered interface that visualizes system health and strategy options. A simulation-based experimental study using a Wizard-of-Oz platform compares conventional manual management with the proposed Human-AI decision support approach. Results show that the framework improves risk detection efficiency, increases decision accuracy, and reduces unnecessary load shedding. The findings demonstrate the potential of human-AI collaboration to enhance situational awareness and decision performance in safety-critical aircraft power management tasks.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Adaptive Performance: Leadership and Decision Autonomy
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational work has implications for employee collaboration, technological demands, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance. This study examines the relationships among leadership vision, employee-AI collaboration, techno-overload, AI overreliance, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance. Cross-sectional survey data from 424 respondents were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that leadership vision is positively associated with employee-AI collaboration and decision autonomy. Employee-AI collaboration is positively associated with AI overreliance, decision autonomy, and adaptive performance, while techno-overload is strongly associated with AI overreliance. Decision autonomy exhibits the strongest direct association with adaptive performance and a significant positive indirect role in the relationship between employee-AI collaboration and adaptive performance. In contrast, the hypothesized negative relationships of techno-overload and AI overreliance with decision autonomy are not supported, nor is the proposed indirect relationship between techno-overload and adaptive performance through decision autonomy. The findings distinguish collaborative AI engagement from reliance-related concerns and highlight the relevance of decision autonomy to employee adaptability. The study contributes to understanding the relationships among organizational leadership, AI-related work experiences, and adaptive performance, offering practical considerations for maintaining employee discretion and responsible AI use in AI-enabled workplaces.

items.title: Integrating iPad-assisted Learning Strategies in High School Science Education: A Critical Narrative Review from a Theoretical Perspective
items.abstract: Tablet computers, and the iPad in particular, have been introduced into secondary schools on a large scale, often through one-to-one programmes justified by claims that portable, touch-based devices will make science learning more engaging, more authentic and more effective. Empirical support for such claims is uneven, and the theoretical reasons why an iPad-assisted activity should or should not improve learning in high school science have rarely been examined together. This critical narrative review synthesises theoretical and empirical literature on iPad-assisted and closely related tablet-assisted learning strategies for students in the upper years of secondary schooling. Literature was identified through structured searches of education-specific and multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, institutional repositories and citation tracking, and was appraised for relevance, design quality and theoretical contribution. The review examines how cognitive load and multimedia learning theory, embodied cognition, inquiry-based and constructivist perspectives, sociocultural and instrumental accounts, generative learning and motivational theory explain the effects of specific strategies, and how integration frameworks such as technological pedagogical content knowledge and the substitution, augmentation, modification and redefinition model have been used, and misused, to guide practice. Strategy-level evidence is strongest for tablets used as experimental tools with multiple linked representations, for well-guided simulations and augmented visualisations, and for student-led or collaborative uses rather than teacher-led display. Meta-analytic averages are generally positive but highly heterogeneous, and they rest heavily on short, small, non-randomised and media-comparison designs, frequently outside the high school age range. Classroom studies repeatedly show that devices are mostly used to replicate existing practice, that teachers' pedagogical knowledge and beliefs condition outcomes, and that distraction, screen-based reading and unequal access remain unresolved concerns. The review proposes an integrative framework in which device affordances influence learning only through specific cognitive, social and motivational mechanisms that are activated by task design, guidance and teacher knowledge. It concludes that the decisive variable is the learning strategy rather than the device, and identifies priorities for theory-testing, longer-term and context-sensitive research.

items.title: Intellectual Tenacity at Work: Generative AI Exposure and the Economic Returns to Occupational Personality Requirements
items.abstract: Technology, including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is changing professional work, but its implications for how occupational personality requirements are rewarded in the labor market remain unclear. Using job-incumbent ratings from the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (O*NET), we identify two personality requirement composites: intellectual tenacity (achievement/effort, persistence, initiative, analytical thinking, innovation, and independence) and social adjustment (emotion regulation, concern for others, social orientation, cooperation, and stress tolerance). We link these measures to more than 15 million workers in the American Community Survey from 2006 to 2024. Intellectual tenacity requirements were positively associated with hourly wages, whereas social adjustment requirements had a weaker, negative association. The wage premium for intellectual tenacity requirements was approximately stable through 2014 and rose thereafter, while the return to social adjustment requirements declined. These divergent trends began before widespread GenAI adoption, but they are concentrated in occupations with greater exposure to GenAI: wage returns for intellectual tenacity requirements increased in occupations highly exposed to GenAI, while returns to social adjustment requirements decreased in those occupations. These findings suggest that broad measures of personality or non-cognitive occupational requirements can obscure opposing shifts in the labor-market value of persistent analytical effort and social adjustment.

items.title: Knowledge Transfer and Talent Development in Traditional Craftsmanship: An HRM Perspective from Atlas Silk
items.abstract: Based on 30 named individual cases documented in public media reports, this paper analyzes the knowledge structure, transmission pathways and talent development challenges associated with Atlas Silk craftsmanship from a human resource management perspective. The B1-B11 framework is used to summarize knowledge content and training arrangements, and the C1-C10 framework is used to identify training, retention and job support issues. The results show that the process and material knowledge can be incorporated into structured training, and the embodied experience of warping, dyeing and weaving still depends on long-term field practice. Families, workshops, cooperatives, colleges and digital communication have complementary functions. To support talent succession, we should combine the phased ability development, compensation guarantee, whole process rotation, dual-mentor training and work design that takes into account the family situation. This paper is a purposively selected literature-based case study, which is not statistically representative.

items.title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
items.abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.

items.title: LLM-Driven Automatic Reward Optimization for Ambient Intelligence Robots with Curriculum Interference Auto-Correction
items.abstract: Service robots in ambient intelligence (AmI) scenarios such as smart factories and home services must rapidly adapt to diverse manipulation tasks, yet traditional reinforcement learning (RL) reward design heavily relies on domain expertise, requiring days to weeks of manual tuning. Existing LLM-assisted reward design methods assume that generated rewards can be directly applied to training environments, overlooking potential incompatibility with built-in training mechanisms such as curriculum learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the signal interference phenomenon between LLM-generated rewards and curriculum dynamic weight adjustments---experiments reveal that curriculum modules amplify penalty weights from an initial $-1\times10^{-4}$ to $-0.1$ (a factor of 1000$\times$), overwhelming the positive reward signals---and it proposes an automatic detection and correction mechanism based on feedback ratio anomaly detection. A unified dual-paradigm framework adapting to both ManagerBasedRL and DirectRL paradigms on the IsaacLab platform, along with a humanized interaction paradigm for non-expert users, are also developed. Systematic experiments on five robot tasks of varying difficulty, including ablation studies, 8-sample random search baselines, and multi-seed statistical tests, demonstrate: on Franka Lift the success rate increases from 0\% to 84\%$\pm$2\% and the mean reward from 0.90 to 84.41$\pm$5.50, where simply disabling the curriculum yields a roughly 5$\times$ increase in mean reward (0.90$\rightarrow$4.47)---a necessary prerequisite for LLM reward optimization to take effect---and combining it with the LLM-designed multi-stage reward structure multiplies the improvement by a further 18.9$\times$; under an equal-compute random-search comparison, LLM weight optimization achieves a 47\% improvement over the best random configuration. Mean-reward ratios depend on the reward definition and should be read together with the scale-invariant success rate. The method reduces reward design time from expert-days to hours, validated on the commercial LLM DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

items.title: LLM-ES: A Multi-Agent Hybrid Framework Integrating Large Language Models and Expert Systems for Autonomous Cyber Defense
items.abstract: In recent years, Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) methods driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance in decision interpretability and environmental transferability, yet suffer from low decision efficiency and unstable decision-making. To mitigate these limitations, this work proposes a multi-agent hybrid LLM–expert system framework for ACD. The framework seamlessly integrates the determinism and efficiency of expert systems with the deep reasoning capabilities of LLMs: the expert system makes deterministic decisions based on experiential knowledge, whereas the LLM is responsible for complex decision tasks demanding deep exploration and long-chain reasoning. We further strengthen the LLM via chain-of-thought (CoT) guided prompting, historical memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), output alignment and feedback learning. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the expert system improves both decision efficiency and defense performance. Evaluated on the CybORG CC4 environment, our approach achieves an average reward of − 98 over ten independent rounds, representing an approximate 25.5% improvement over the best-performing reinforcement learning (RL) baseline. Compared with the standalone LLM method, the average reward increases by roughly 96.2%, while the average per-step runtime is reduced by approximately 14.6%. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically integrate LLMs and expert systems for ACD in the CybORG CC4 environment.

items.title: Measuring the Hermeneutic Circle in Explainable AI: A Human-Free Test Based on Data Horizons, Executable Claims, Part–Whole Agreement, and Machine Readers
items.abstract: Explanations of machine learning models are read by people but rarely evaluated with them, and automatic metrics score attribution vectors rather than what a reader receives. We operationalise the horizon, the hermeneutic circle, and the hermeneutics of suspicion as the Hermeneutic Circle Test (HCT), a human-free screen for explanations of tabular classifiers. HCT checks whether an explanation’s evidence lies inside a calibrated data horizon, whether its sentences survive on-horizon interventions, whether its account of a case agrees with the whole model and at which scale, and whether it helps machine readers learn the model. Over seven explainers, four datasets, and two model families (mean ± standard deviation over eight settings), the best explainer, KernelSHAP, verified 0.65 ± 0.15 of its claims, while random attributions verified 0.22 ± 0.08. On the same explanations, established faithfulness, remove-and-retrain, and disagreement metrics missed impossible evidence and narratives contradicting their own attributions, and sign-blind metrics scored sign-flipped explanations like the originals. Claim tests withstood scaffold attacks that adapt to the horizon and to the test itself; a scaffold that memorises the audited records weakened them and deceived every explainer, but part–whole agreement still flagged it. HCT is a reproducible screen to apply before user studies.

items.title: Mechanism Design and Active Systems Theory: 60 Years of Parallel Development
items.abstract: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.

items.title: Mediating role of AI-Human Collaboration in the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Employee Performance
items.abstract: This study examines the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on employee performance in selected Federal Teaching Hospitals and Federal Medical Centres in Nigeria, with a focus on the mediating role of AI-Human Collaboration. A cross-sectional research design was adopted. The population comprised clinical and non-clinical healthcare workers in selected public healthcare institutions in Nigeria. Using a multistage sampling technique 520 questionnaires were distributed, of which 371 valid responses were analyzed. SmartPLS 4 was employed for data analysis. Findings reveal that AI adoption significantly enhances both AIhuman collaboration and employee performance. AI-human collaboration also has a significant positive effect on employee performance and significantly mediates the relationship between AI adoption and employee performance. The study concludes that AI adoption improves employee performance both directly and indirectly through enhanced collaboration between employees and AI systems. It recommends that healthcare institutions should strengthen AI-human collaboration through continuous training and integration of AI technologies to maximize performance outcomes. These measures are essential for improving workforce efficiency and achieving sustainable performance in Nigeria’s healthcare sector.

items.title: Methodology for Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Chatbots: A Review with Applications to Agricultural Advisory Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence chatbots increasingly advise farmers, yet their adoption should rest on rigorous, standardised evaluation. This review brings together five standardised instruments for assessing chatbots (the System Usability Scale, the Chatbot Usability Scale, the Checklist for Trust between People and Automation, the AI Chatbots Usage Scale, and the User Engagement Scale) and one assessment method, knowledge testing. It also explains Cronbach’s alpha, the reliability criterion most of them rely on. A case study from the literature, in which five large language models answered PhD-level soil science questions, together with deployed systems such as Farmer.Chat and AgroLLM, show how evaluation works in practice and why fluent but unverified advice is risky. Beyond questionnaires, we examine accuracy-based and retrieval-grounded testing. We propose a five-layer protocol that first checks technical accuracy, then usability, trust, engagement, and learning outcomes, to guide the design and validation of chatbots for precision and smallholder farming.
